opus-5.5.text:
I think the core problem is that these benchmarks became the goal instead of a tool. Atari and MuJoCo were great at the start. They gave everyone a shared, cheap, reproducible testbed, and that helped the field get going. But after a while people were mostly tuning algorithms to squeeze a few more points out of the same set of games or locomotion tasks. A lot of papers end up with gains that are within the noise. They depend on hyperparameters, seeds, or implementation details more than on the idea itself. I saw this firsthand working on RL libraries. Small things like observation normalization, how you handle timeouts, or the details of advantage computation can matter more than the "novel" algorithmic contribution.

The second issue is that these environments don't look like the problems that actually matter now. In the real world, especially with large language models, the bottleneck usually isn't a clever new policy gradient variant. It's infrastructure. Can you run rollouts at scale, keep the system stable, design good reward signals, and iterate quickly? Academic benchmarks hide all of that. The environment is tiny and the reward is given to you for free. So the skills you build optimizing Atari scores don't transfer well to training a real system.

There's also a speed problem. Many academic setups were bottlenecked by slow environment simulation, and that's partly why I worked on things like faster parallel environment execution. If one experiment takes days, you can't explore much, so people end up making incremental tweaks rather than asking bigger questions.

So my view is that academic RL needs to move toward problems with real stakes and real scale, and to value engineering and infrastructure as first-class research. The interesting RL problems today are about making learning work in messy, large, open-ended settings, and it's worth more to get those right than to gain half a percent on HalfCheetah.

r001.rationale: The response says researchers tuned algorithms for marginal gains on the same Atari games and locomotion tasks, making the benchmarks the goal rather than a tool.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the core problem is that these benchmarks quietly became the goal instead of the measuring stick. Atari and MuJoCo were great when they came out, because they gave everyone a shared yardstick. But over time the field started optimizing for the yardstick itself.

A few things happen when that goes on long enough. First, you get algorithms that are heavily tuned to the quirks of the benchmark. People will spend months squeezing another few percent out of Breakout or HalfCheetah, and a lot of that gain comes from hyperparameter search, seed selection, or implementation tricks rather than a genuinely new idea. When I was working on Tianshou, I saw this constantly. You reimplement a paper faithfully and the numbers don't match, and then you discover the gap is some small engineering detail that was never written down. That tells you the reported improvement was fragile to begin with.

Second, these environments are cheap to simulate and fully observable, with clean reward signals. Real problems are almost never like that. Rewards are sparse or delayed, the simulator is expensive or doesn't exist, and the state is partial and noisy. So a method that looks dominant on MuJoCo may give you no signal about whether it will work in robotics, in dialogue, or in anything with a human in the loop. We have been selecting for the wrong properties.

Third, there is a reproducibility and infrastructure problem that the benchmark culture hides. Papers compare against baseline numbers copied from other papers, run with different codebases, different frame counts, different evaluation protocols. The variance across random seeds on these tasks is often larger than the claimed improvement. So a lot of the "progress" on the leaderboard is noise that nobody has the incentive to clean up, because the incentive is to publish.

I'd also say the benchmarks shaped what questions people asked. Sample efficiency on Atari became a whole subfield, but the honest question was whether you can scale compute and data, and whether the method transfers. Once you move toward things like RL with human feedback for language models, the bottleneck is not the algorithm at all. It is the reward model, the data, the infrastructure for running thousands of rollouts reliably, and the engineering to keep training stable. Almost none of that is exercised by Atari.

So I don't think the benchmarks were a mistake. They were necessary. The mistake was treating saturation on them as the finish line, rather than asking what the next environment should be that actually stresses the properties we care about.

r001.rationale: The response says researchers began optimizing for Atari and MuJoCo benchmark quirks and treating saturation on those tasks as the finish line, clearly describing overfitting to a narrow benchmark set.

astra-6.text:
I think the problem is that doing well on a benchmark can become the goal, rather than a way to measure progress. In Atari or MuJoCo, you have a well-defined environment, a reward function, and the ability to collect lots of experience. Those are useful conditions for studying algorithms, but they leave out many of the challenges you face in a real application.

In practice, you have to figure out what to reward, whether you can safely explore, and how to learn when data is expensive or the environment changes. So a method that improves a benchmark score doesn’t necessarily address the thing preventing someone from using reinforcement learning. I’d like to see more research start with an actual problem and let that problem determine what we need to solve.

r001.rationale: The response says benchmark performance can become the goal and explains that Atari and MuJoCo omit many real application challenges, conveying that research is overly focused on this narrow set of benchmark tasks.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the problem is that we can become very good at solving the benchmark without solving the problems that make reinforcement learning useful in the real world. In Atari or MuJoCo, you have a simulator, a reward function, and the ability to collect a lot of experience. In a real application, those are often the hard parts: Where does the reward come from? How much interaction can you afford? What happens when the environment changes?

Those benchmarks are useful for comparing ideas, but a higher score doesn’t necessarily mean we’ve made progress on those questions. I’d like to see more research start from an actual problem and let its constraints drive the algorithm.

r001.rationale: The response says researchers can become very good at solving benchmarks such as Atari and MuJoCo without solving real-world problems, and recommends letting real problems drive research. This clearly conveys overfitting to benchmark tasks.
